criterion_notes.c1: Examines household access to central piped water connections and full service (central water connection, central sewerage connection, and electricity) across urban localities in Brazil, focusing on small (1-3 room) houses occupied by low-income migrants and informal/untitled housing.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, this clearly qualifies (yes): the paper examines municipal exclusionary infrastructure policies, inter-jurisdictional strategic governance across fragmented metropolitan municipalities, pre- vs. post-1988 legal reforms governing infrastructure provision to informal settlements, housing tenure/land title, and municipal minimum lot-size zoning regulations (>125 sq m). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, it also qualifies (yes, though somewhat indirect in the main regressions): rather than generic project delivery, behavioural promotion, or unanalysed macro-governance background, the paper analyzes (1) municipal administrative discretion and strategic exclusionary withholding of central water connections from low-income/informal housing (enabled in the 1980s by legal rules prohibiting public water and sewer provision to untitled favelas and zoning-noncompliant loteamentos, and tested against a 2000 counterfactual after post-1988 legal reforms lifted restrictions on servicing informal settlements), (2) tenure/documentation status (comparing 1991 water and sewer connection rates across titled homeowners vs. homeowners without land title and squatter/ceded housing, and using water connections among untitled homes in robustness checks), and (3) decentralized multi-municipality metropolitan regulatory structure enabling strategic inter-municipal competition in water provision (W'b reaction functions). Note that the Section 4 regressions operationalize exclusionary municipal policy through spatial reaction functions, locality income-by-size interactions, and 1991 vs. 2000 regime counterfactuals rather than a direct municipal connection-ordinance dummy.
criterion_notes.c3: Quantitative empirical econometric study analyzing Brazilian Population Census data (1970, 1980, 1991, 2000), IBGE municipal land-use regulation surveys (1999, 2005), 1982 legislative election returns, and geological/insolation instrumental variables across up to 447 localities (MCAs) in 123 urban areas, using OLS with urban-area fixed effects, spatial-lag/spatial-error MLE, district-fixed-effects hedonic regressions, and 2SLS/LIML estimation.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports multiple directly relevant outcomes: (1) locality-level share of small houses (1-2 rooms in 1980; 1-3 rooms in 1991 and 2000), large houses, and untitled houses connected to a central water system and full service (central water, central sewer, electricity); (2) hedonic rental price premia (willingness-to-pay) for central water and central sewer connections in Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro; and (3) demographic exclusion/deflection of migrant and low-educated households across localities from 1991 to 2000.
criterion_notes.c5: Population, unit of analysis (Minimum Comparable Areas / localities within urban areas, plus rental housing units in Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro), exposures, outcomes, and econometric study design are all clearly identified in the 38 pages of body text and Appendix A. Note that the appended table/figure pages (PDF pages 39-46, 48, 50) had no extractable text in the cached PDF, which may limit full tabular extraction for meta-analysis (Criterion 6 synthesis gate), but key sample sizes, descriptive shares, and regression point estimates are explicitly reported in the text.

evidence_quotes.quote: Richer and larger localities in an urban area reduce provision of water and sewerage connections to the smaller houses in which poorer migrants would live to discourage the in-migration of these poorer migrants and deflect them to other localities.

A key aspect is that until the late 1980s and democratization, it was in principle “illegal” for localities to provide public infrastructure such as central sewer and water connections in either type of settlement. This gave an opportunistic excuse to deny or limit such provision.
One set of reforms removed restrictions on localities providing infrastructure to the informal sector; another encouraged the regularization of informal housing sectors and the upgrading of services.
Not surprisingly, the worst served are those who report that they do not own the land under their house.

We have Brazilian Population Census data for 1970, 1980, 1991 and 2000. These data contain a variety of information on housing size, tenure mode, and servicing of houses as well as basic socioeconomic information covering education, income, family structure, and migration.
In 1980, only 61% of small houses in our localities had a water connection while 86% of large houses had a water connection.

raw_response.exposure: Strategic municipal exclusionary infrastructure policy and local administrative discretion in withholding water connections (measured via inter-municipal spatial reaction functions to neighboring localities' servicing rates W'b, locality income-by-size interactions, 1982 anti-military vote share, and pre-1988 dictatorship vs. post-1988 democratization legal reforms lifting restrictions on servicing informal settlements), alongside household land-title/tenure status and municipal minimum lot-size zoning laws (>125 sq m); in growth regressions, locality central water connection share for small (1-3 room) and untitled houses in 1991
raw_response.outcome: Share of urban households and small (1-3 room) houses (as well as large houses and untitled houses) connected to a central piped water system and full service (central water, central sewer, and electricity) in 1970-2000; hedonic rental price premia for central water and central sewer connections in 1980; and locality household population growth rate (overall and by low- vs. high-educated household heads, reflecting demographic exclusion/deflection of migrants) from 1991 to 2000
raw_response.population_and_sample: Urban households (disaggregated by house size such as 1-3 room small houses vs. 7-9 room large houses, housing tenure/land title status, migration status, and household head education) across 447 localities (Minimum Comparable Areas, MCAs, comprising 659 municipalities in 1991) in 123 Brazilian urban areas from 1970 to 2000 (main econometric sample: 351 predominantly urban MCAs in 55 multi-locality urban areas; restricted strategic sample: 23 urban areas with 2-3 localities), plus rental housing units across 56 districts in Sao Paulo and 24 districts in Rio de Janeiro in 1980
raw_response.rationale: This NBER working paper empirically examines exclusionary municipal water and sewerage connection policies in urban Brazil (1970-2000). It satisfies all inclusion criteria: it studies household central water and sewerage connection rates (c1, c4) using multi-decade Brazilian Census microdata/aggregates and econometric models (OLS with urban-area fixed effects, spatial MLE, hedonic regressions, and 2SLS/LIML IV) (c3, c5) in English (c6). For Criterion 2, it satisfies both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism scope by analyzing strategic municipal discretion to withhold water connections from low-income/informal housing (enabled pre-1988 by legal rules prohibiting public water/sewer provision to untitled favelas and zoning-noncompliant loteamentos and contrasted against a 2000 counterfactual after post-1988 legal reforms lifted those restrictions), alongside census comparisons of water/sewer connections by land-title/tenure status and municipal >125 sq m lot-size zoning laws. Confidence is set to medium because the Section 4 regressions operationalize exclusionary municipal discretion indirectly (via spatial reaction functions, income-by-size interactions, and 1991 vs. 2000 regime counterfactuals rather than a direct municipal connection-rule indicator) and because the PDF's appended table pages (pages 39-46, 48, 50) lacked extracted text, although the 38 pages of prose report full methods, sample sizes, shares, and key regression estimates.
raw_response.study_design: Observational longitudinal and cross-sectional econometric study (panel census data with urban-area fixed effects, spatial autoregressive maximum likelihood, district-fixed-effects hedonic regressions, and 2SLS/LIML instrumental variables)
